facts.statement: Ocepesuchus possessed a long snout with a tubular shape that was wider than it was high.
facts.quote: Ocepesuchus had a long snout with a tubular shape, wider than high.

facts.statement: Based on its narrow snout, Ocepesuchus likely had a piscivorous diet, but its skull, preserved at about 38 cm long, was too small to eat large pycnodonts like Phacodus.
facts.quote: Ocepesuchus likely had a piscivorous diet based on its narrow snout, but it wasn't suited for eating large pycnodonts like Phacodus, with the preserved portion of its skull measuring only about 38 cm long.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the type specimen was either a small adult or subadult that may have spent juvenile stages in freshwater, potentially offering some protection from the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
facts.quote: The type specimen is interpreted as either a small-sized adult or a subadult, and it may have spent its time in freshwater during its juvenile stages, similar to modern marine crocodiles; if this were indeed the case, some of the juveniles may have been protected to an extent from the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.

facts.statement: A cladistic analysis by Jouve and colleagues classified Ocepesuchus as a gavialoid.
facts.quote: Jouve and colleagues performed a cladistic analysis incorporating their new taxon, and found Ocepesuchus to be a gavialoid.

facts.statement: Ocepesuchus lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)
